### Anita Brookner Is the Book of the Week, Haymitch Divides the Critics and Delights the Audience, and Two Detectives Cross the Sea

Filed as: Sunday Review of Reviews — Weekend Features · 2026-11-22T04:10:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-22-sunday-reviews.html

Weekend Features — Sunday Review of Reviews

 Objective

 Anita Brookner Is the Book of the Week, Haymitch Divides the Critics and Delights the Audience, and Two Detectives Cross the Sea

 The week's review lists were tallied, and the tally gave the desk a book with no dissent in its count and a screen week divided by audience. The book du jour is Anita Brookner: Art and Life by Hermione Lee, published by Knopf on November 17: first in the week's nonfiction tally with twelve rave reviews and four positive, and no mixed or negative verdict recorded—a biography of a novelist who destroyed her papers, said she would leave no trace, and would, by every reviewer's account, have hated being biographied. On screen, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opened November 20 with the critics at 67 to 72 percent and verified audiences at 95 percent, the two camps agreeing on Joseph Zada's young Haymitch and dividing on whether the prequel needed to exist; and The Blue Road, the Korea-Japan crime serial on Netflix, released the same day in eight episodes, drew 9 of 10, 8 of 10 and 4.5 of 5 for the chemistry of its two detectives, a Seoul man and a Tokyo man working one serial killer across the sea between them. The desk states its position plainly at the head of each part: it has not read the book, and it has not watched the film or the serial. What follows is a review of reviews.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0410 ET, Sunday, November 22, 2026. The third Sunday Review of Reviews of this paper, filed under the Weekend Features ruling of November 4, 2026. The desk tallied the week's review lists—the New York Times Book Review and its peers, the Washington reviewing tradition carried in Ron Charles's Tuesday Review, the Guardian, and the aggregating tally at Book Marks—and the week's film and television reviews, international by house rule. The clippings the report was drawn from are filed beneath it, each stamped subjective.

The Week in Brief: The Tally

In nonfiction, one book stood clear of the whole week's lists, in both halves of the tally combined. Book Marks' tally of the week, published November 20, ranks Anita Brookner: Art and Life by Hermione Lee first in nonfiction with twelve rave reviews and four positive—sixteen counted reviews, none of them mixed and none negative, the largest clean count the desk has recorded in this feature. Behind it: Gerald Martin's Mario Vargas Llosa: A Life, five rave, two positive and two mixed; Gary Shteyngart's The Sensualist, four rave and one positive; Paul Goldberger's The Imperfect City, three rave and two positive; and Jennifer Croft's Notes on Postcards, two rave and two positive. In fiction the tally is led by Nick Harkaway's The Taper Man: A Novel of John le Carr&eacute;'s Circus, at five rave, one positive and one mixed, followed by Tahmima Anam's Uprising at four rave, one positive and one mixed, K Chiucarello's Nanny Nanny at one rave and three positive, Scarlett Thomas's The Runner at one rave, two positive and two mixed, and Cleo Birdwell's Amazons at one rave, three positive, one mixed and one pan.

The week's selected single reviews carry the same two names at the top, and the desk files the agreement. The five reviews Literary Hub selected on November 19 include Amy Davidson Sorkin on Joe Biden's Promise Me, America, Anahid Nersessian on Edith Hall's Medea: A Life, and George Packer on Bob Woodward's Secrets, among its five; the week's best-reviewed list, carried by the same house, names Shteyngart, Harkaway and Brookner in its headline. The book du jour therefore stands on the tally's arithmetic, which is this paper's method: twelve raves is not a close call, and the desk prints the book the count chose, while filing the fiction leader, The Taper Man, in its own paragraph below.

Part One — The Book: Anita Brookner: Art and Life, by Hermione Lee

The desk has not read this book. It says so plainly, as the house rule requires: everything in this part is what the reviewers report, agree on, and dispute, and nothing in it is the desk's reading. Anita Brookner: Art and Life is a biography. Hermione Lee is the biographer of Virginia Woolf, Edith Wharton, Penelope Fitzgerald and Tom Stoppard. Her subject, Anita Brookner (1928–2016), was an art historian at the Courtauld Institute who published her first novel at 53, won the Booker Prize in 1984 for her fourth novel, Hotel du Lac, and wrote 25 novels in all. This book was published in the United States by Knopf on November 17, 2026: 544 pages, $45, ISBN 9780593321508.

On what the book must overcome, the reviewers agree completely, and their agreement is the week's firmest fact. Brookner disposed of her letters, left no private papers, warned interviewers she would stamp on any attempt at a biography, and said, in the words the reviews repeat, “I shall leave no trace.” She died in 2016 at 87. Lee herself, in the line every review quotes, concedes the position: “How she would have hated having a biography!” The reviewers also agree on the life the biography assembles from what remains: born in 1928 in Herne Hill, the only child of Polish Jewish &eacute;migr&eacute; parents—her father in the tobacco business, her mother a failed singer—formed as a postgraduate researcher in postwar Paris, and established first as an electrifying art historian before the fiction began. And they agree on the caricature Lee writes against: the melancholy, cigarette-smoking recluse in a long grey cardigan, wistfully yearning for an absent or unreliable lover—the “aloof spinster” of the reductive notices, churning out the same novel every July.

On what the book is taken to be, the favorable reviews—sixteen of the sixteen counted—agree in substance and differ only in temperature. Leigh Haber in the Boston Globe, in the passage the tally carries, calls it a passionate case for studying a complex, compelling, now obscure figure, a connoisseur of women's interior lives who could see what many did not, and holds that for readers who have felt similarly dismissed the biography may spark a new passion for her. Kathryn Hughes in Literary Review calls it a flawless biography, fond but not foolish, whose rigour never simply equates the heroines with their creator: Brookner emerges spikier, sharper, cooler than anyone had noticed. The Guardian's Lucy Atkins, in the praise filed with the book, calls it an astute and tireless biography that succeeds, against the odds, in unearthing an author who would be appalled by the scrutiny. Kirkus, in its starred notice, calls it majestic, a deeply researched, empathetic portrayal; Publishers Weekly, also starred, calls it masterful, a captivating reevaluation of a singular and enigmatic novelist. The shared claim under the praise is Lee's own, as the reviews report it: Brookner was not her heroines but their inventor—a deeply romantic and passionate writer whose armour was an austere, controlled manner, a dry formal vocabulary and a scathing wit—and her 25 novels are read, in Lee's proposal carried by Bookforum, not as repetitions but as versions of one long Proustian book, as Monet repainted Rouen Cathedral.

The split in the file is about length, and it is filed by the two largest American notices against the British consensus. The New York Times review, as Book Marks excerpts it, holds that Brookner is the subject of a new, 500-page book from the tenacious and indefatigable Lee, and that at half the length Anita Brookner: Art and Life would probably have been twice as good: it is padded in ways that add drag to its stately propulsion, forced into detours and workarounds because relatively little is known of Brookner's private life, and consuming it can be like reading the introduction to a reissue that goes on for hundreds of pages—while conceding, in the same notice, that the book is very, very good in places, with terrific vividness. A second American account filed with the tally calls the biography deft and adulatory, and names the challenge the Times presses: what is a biographer to do when the subject does nothing much but write? The Times of London files a narrower version of the same reservation from inside its praise: Lee brings rigour and authority, refuses the melancholy caricature, and the narrative suffers in the second half, through the dutiful summaries of the 25 novels, where Lee herself observes that some later works burn on a low flame and can be repetitive and prolix. The desk files the disagreement as it stands. No reviewer in the week's file disputes Lee's research, her subject's worth, or the portrait's direction; the dispute is whether 544 pages is the portrait's frame or its padding.

The fiction leader is filed in one paragraph, as the tally's second book. The Taper Man, Nick Harkaway's second George Smiley novel after Karla's Choice (2024), is set in 1965: a British agent is shot in Helsinki, the Circus's prize asset in Moscow is imperilled, and the trail leads Smiley to Los Angeles and a sleeper agent—the taper man, left behind to keep the candle lit—poised to expose the asset. Publishers Weekly, in the passage the tally carries, holds that the conclusion is anything but conclusive, as in most of the Circus novels, and that Harkaway exhibits his father's knack for slow reveals, complex storylines and salient observations about human nature: George Smiley is in good hands. Ron Charles, in his Tuesday Review, records being captivated even when lost, credits the book with exposing the prejudices that infected America's intelligence establishment—a brilliant African American woman sidelined for her skin colour, and the strategic cost of it—and files Smiley wincing through the heat and ugliness of Los Angeles as terrific fun. The tally counts five rave, one positive and one mixed.

Where to get it. Anita Brookner: Art and Life by Hermione Lee is available at Amazon. As an Amazon Associate, Objective Daily News earns from qualifying purchases made through that link.

Part Two — Screen: Haymitch at 95 Percent, and Two Detectives Cross the Sea

The desk has not watched any of the screen works in this part. It has not sat in a cinema for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, and it has not streamed The Blue Road or I Play Rocky. Their status here is the same as the book's: the reviews, reviewed.

The television pick of the week is The Blue Road, and it is a Korea-Japan serial, and it opened the same day as the week's film. The eight-episode crime serial—Pureungil in Korean—was released on Netflix on November 20, directed by Han Jun-hee, who also directed D.P. and the recent Dead-End Job, and co-written with Cho Yu-jin. It is adapted from the 2002 comic Blue Road by Keishi Edogawa and Kwon Ka-ya, and it is set in 2002, the year Japan and South Korea co-hosted the World Cup. Son Suk-ku plays Kim Seok, a Seoul detective; Eita Nagayama plays Hiroshi Inose, a Tokyo detective; a serial killer is killing in both countries, and the two men, who meet in a chase and dislike each other on sight, must work one case across the sea. Kim Shin-rok, Choi Sung-eun, Jung Jae-young and Kentaro Sakaguchi stand in the cast the reviews name. The first three episodes screened at the Busan International Film Festival ahead of release, to positive reviews in the accounts filed below.

The reviewers agree on the pairing, on the grip, and on what the case is carrying. Every review in the file credits the same centre: the chemistry of Son and Nagayama, a hard-boiled, no-nonsense Seoul detective carrying a violent past and a more open, easygoing Tokyo detective whose passion for the work keeps breaking through, the contrast turning an uneasy collaboration into a bond the reviewers root for. Every review records the same construction under the case: the wounds of Japan's historical impact on Korea, still lingering, worked through the partnership itself, so that the investigation carries the two countries' history as well as their killer. And every review records the victims' staging and the messages left with them as genuinely unsettling, the horror delivered, in the opening murder, mostly through sound. The scores print the agreement without ornament: But Why Tho? at 9 of 10, calling the serial rich and compelling and a must-watch for crime drama fans; Pixel Twelve at 8 of 10 for the opening three episodes; K-Waves and Beyond at 4.5 of 5; Leisurebyte calling it one of the best crime thrillers its reviewer has watched this year.

The split is small, and the desk files it at its true size. One review names the score as its one complaint—generic thriller work sitting in the background, partly redeemed by the killer intro. But Why Tho?, in its 9 of 10 notice, records a last-minute callback in the final episode that is more sentimental than earned. Leisurebyte records that the opening episode needs a few minutes to build momentum before the serial becomes relentless, and that the killer is identified by the fourth episode, the interest thereafter lying in the complexities the case opens rather than in the whodunit. No review in the file faults the two leads, the period setting, or the handling of the history. The desk files the week's television record as the screen week's one consensus: a brutal serial-killer case carried, by agreement, on a partnership.

In cinemas, the week's film is The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, and its reviewers agree on its Haymitch and divide on its existence. The film opened November 20, directed by Francis Lawrence, rated PG-13 and running 158 minutes—the longest in the franchise, in the weekend accounts—with Joseph Zada as the young Haymitch Abernathy, the District 12 victor of the 50th Hunger Games, the Second Quarter Quell, 24 years before the original films, in the story Suzanne Collins published in 2025. Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin and Elle Fanning stand in the cast the reviews name. The agreement in the file is exact and runs through reviews that agree on nothing else: Zada is the film's asset. The Hollywood Reporter's David Rooney calls his Haymitch a breakout performance—invested with tenacity, kindness and heartrending vulnerability—and a far more poignant and involving origin story than young Snow's in the previous prequel; IndieWire's Ryan Lattanzio, against his own verdict on the film, credits Zada in the same role; RogerEbert.com's account lists Zada alongside Woody Harrelson as the actors defining the character across the saga. The craft agreement runs beside it: Jo Willems's muscular camerawork, James Newton Howard's soaring score and Uli Hanisch's imaginative production design, credited by name in the favorable and the mixed notices alike.

The division is the prequel itself, and the counts print it in two currencies. Rooney calls the film a worthier prequel that delivers on emotion and brutal spectacle. Against him, the Guardian's Peter Bradshaw, at one star, holds that the film has no actual interest and no authentic reason to exist other than to gouge an income stream out of its fanbase. Between the poles: the New York Times' Brandon Yu finds a film both bloated and limited, cloistered in its vision of the games and the wider world, its formula named as dystopian pulp, doomed romance, teenage heroism and rebellion; Variety's Owen Gleiberman finds it meandering and more than a bit thin, directed in the lavish mode he calls Hunger Games Classic; IndieWire finds it overlong, visually soupy and narratively morose. The critics' counts moved as the file arrived: 75 percent in one early count, 72 percent from 71 reviews in a second, 69 percent from 62 in a third, 67 percent on opening day and 68 percent on Saturday, with Metacritic at 56. The audience count did not move in the same way: 95 percent from verified moviegoers—a franchise record, ahead of Catching Fire at 89 percent—with an A-minus CinemaScore and PostTrak at 93 percent positive. The box office filed the same shape in dollars: $56 million on Friday including $21.25 million in Thursday previews, a projection of $120 million or more for the weekend, and the No. 1 position in 66 of the 67 markets it had opened in. The desk files the split as it stands: the people who review films respect this one more than they love it, and the people who bought tickets love it more than any Hunger Games film before it.

The week's second film is filed in one paragraph, because its scores run the other way from the week's headline film in degree, not in shape. I Play Rocky, the account of how Sylvester Stallone made Rocky, expanded wide on November 20 to about 2,000 theatres, one day before the 50th anniversary of the original film's 1976 release, after a limited run that averaged $17,024 per theatre. The weekend guide filed below records it at 87 percent certified fresh with critics and 98 percent with audiences—this weekend's best scores by a wide margin, in that account—with tracking toward an opening of about $12 million. The desk has not seen either film; it files the week's cinema record as two audience leads of different sizes, one of them a franchise record.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, Haymitch's score: Sunrise on the Reaping stands at 75 percent in an early count, 72 percent from 71 reviews, 69 percent from 62 reviews, 67 percent on opening day and 68 percent on Saturday, with Metacritic at 56—a film whose critics' measure moves because the review file is still arriving, printed here as a moving measure against an audience measure, 95 percent, that every count agrees on. Second, the Blue Road's source and its detective's name: Dramabeans describes the original as a 2002 manhwa of the same name, But Why Tho? as a manhwa adapted into a K-drama, and the Bangla Pulse lineup as adapted from a 2002 comic; the lead actor is Sohn Seok-gu in Dramabeans' spelling, Son Suk-ku in the Netflix reviews, and Son Sukku in two of them; and the episode length stands at about 45 minutes in one account and 45 to 55 minutes in another. The desk prints the spellings and the counts as their sources filed them. Third, the book's length: the publisher's record and Bookforum give Anita Brookner: Art and Life at 544 pages, and the New York Times review, as excerpted, describes a 500-page book; the desk prints the publisher's 544 as the book's record and the Times' figure as its review's. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts are single-valued: Anita Brookner: Art and Life was published in the United States on November 17, 2026, by Knopf, at 544 pages and $45, and stands first in the week's nonfiction tally at twelve rave and four positive; The Taper Man stands first in fiction at five rave, one positive and one mixed; The Blue Road was released on Netflix on November 20 in eight episodes; and Sunrise on the Reaping and I Play Rocky both opened wide on November 20. The desk has not read the book and has not watched the screen works. The log proceeds to Sunday's watches.

 The Clippings Filed With This Feature

 Everything the desk read for the feature above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk's feature is the only item in this file stamped objective. 21 items.

In fiction, Nick Harkaway's The Taper Man stands first at five rave, one positive and one mixed; Tahmima Anam's Uprising follows at four rave, one positive and one mixed, and K Chiucarello's Nanny Nanny stands third at one rave and three positive.  SubjectiveBook Marks — reviews of Anita Brookner: Art and LifeThe Book Marks page for the biography records its publisher and date—Knopf, November 17, 2026—and a rating of four of four across sixteen reviews. It excerpts Leigh Haber of the Boston Globe, for whom Lee offers a passionate case for studying a complex, compelling, now obscure figure; the New York Times review, for which Brookner is the subject of a 500-page book from the tenacious and indefatigable Lee, at half the length twice as good, padded in ways that add drag to its stately propulsion and very, very good in places; and a third notice calling the biography deft and adulatory, assembling what facts there are while exposing the challenge of a subject who does nothing much but write.

 SubjectiveThe Times — the life of Anita Brookner, the 'aloof spinster' who wrote Hotel du LacJohanna Thomas-Corr's review opens before Lee's first sentence, on her epigraph from Brookner's fifteenth novel: the dead, perhaps even more than the living, have a right to their mysteries. Brookner warned she would stamp on any attempt at a biography, disposed of her letters and left no private papers. Lee, the review holds, refuses the melancholy caricature of the cigarette-smoking recluse in a long grey cardigan and pursues instead an electrifying art historian and a deeply romantic and passionate writer, born in 1928 in Herne Hill to Polish Jewish &eacute;migr&eacute; parents and formed in postwar Paris; the narrative suffers in the second half, through dutiful summaries of the 25 novels, some of which Lee herself finds repetitive and prolix.

 SubjectiveLiterary Review — Kathryn Hughes: spiky, sharp, coolKathryn Hughes calls Lee's biography flawless, fond but not foolish: Brookner, who died in 2016 at 87, would have hated a biography, and Lee is too honest to pretend she dithered when the agent and literary executor proposed it. Lee's rigour never simply equates the novelist's heroines with their creator, and Brookner emerges as a considerably more subtle and varied author than she has generally been given credit for: spikier, sharper, cooler than anyone had noticed. The review records the breakthrough of Hotel du Lac, Booker Prize winner in 1984, and Lee's particular strength on Brookner's postgraduate years in Paris.

 SubjectiveBookforum — the dour and the gloryBookforum's account lists the book from Knopf at 544 pages and $45, and takes Lee's project as an argument: to show a life-changing writer, nonpareil stylist, courageous thinker and extraordinary human being, a deeply romantic and passionate writer whose armour is an austere, controlled manner, a dry formal vocabulary and a scathing wit. It carries Lee's proposal that the late novels are versions of one long Proustian book, as Monet repainted Rouen Cathedral and C&eacute;zanne returned to Mont Sainte-Victoire, and records the two common critiques of Brookner the biography answers: too many books, and too much bleakness.

 SubjectivePenguin Random House — Anita Brookner by Hermione Lee, the publisher's recordThe publisher's page records the book as a hardcover from Knopf, published November 17, 2026, 544 pages, $45, ISBN 9780593321508, and describes its subject in its own copy: Brookner is famous for her quiet, incisive studies of solitary and emotionally restrained characters, often middle-class women navigating loneliness, disappointment and small eruptions of desire beneath a fa&ccedil;ade of reserve.

 SubjectiveBut Why Tho? — The Blue Road review: a rich and compelling crime dramaBut Why Tho? scores the serial 9 of 10: the wounds left by Japan's historical impact on Korea linger, and the serial picks apart the fragile nature of Japanese-Korean relations through its detective pairing, set in 2002 during the co-hosted World Cup. It opens with a murder in Japan delivered mostly through sound, a Hangul message above the victim, and a camera snap that introduces Son Suk-ku's Kim Seok to Eita Nagayama's Inose. Son and Nagayama make, in its verdict, a magical pairing, the serial incredibly gripping from beginning to end, its one reservation a last-minute callback in the final episode that is more sentimental than earned.

 SubjectiveLeisurebyte — The Blue Road review: a gripping Korean-Japanese crime thrillerLeisurebyte takes the serial as a tightly paced crime thriller balancing brutality with buddy-cop chemistry: two detectives try to find a serial killer and stumble on a war that goes back years and brings everyone's identity into question. Son Suk-ku is fantastic as the hard-boiled Kim Seok, haunted by a violent past, and Eita Nagayama adds a welcome change of pace as the more easygoing Inose; the killer is identified by the fourth episode, and the interest thereafter lies in the complexities of crime in the two countries and the way it unites them. Its verdict: an arresting thriller, difficult to stop watching once the opening episode builds its momentum.

Son is superb under a composed persona, Nagayama's humour and friendlier nature refresh the darkness without taking away its gravity, the victims' staging and the killer's messages build a highly ominous environment, and the visual aspect is, in its account, just as amazing.

 SubjectiveTito Gamer — The Blue Road review: the buddy-cop thriller I couldn't stop watchingThe Tito Gamer review records all eight episodes out since November 20, 2026, at about 45 minutes each, directed by Han Jun-hee and based on Blue Road, a 2002 Korea-Japan comic by Keishi Edogawa and Kwon Ka-ya, with Son Suk-ku as Kim Seok of Seoul and Eita Nagayama as Hiroshi Inose of Tokyo and Kentaro Sakaguchi owning some of the creepiest scenes. Its verdict: dark, sharp and more human than expected, a partnership believed from episode one and a mystery that keeps digging deeper; its one complaint is the score, generic thriller work in the background, partly redeemed by the killer intro.

 SubjectiveParade — Hunger Games moviegoers left in tears as critics deliver blow on Rotten TomatoesParade, published November 21, records Sunrise on the Reaping opening November 20 at 67 percent on Rotten Tomatoes against 95 percent from verified moviegoers, a gap of 28 points. Critics questioned whether the franchise has anything new to offer, citing pacing, length, reliance on familiar characters and the handling of the Arena deaths in the Second Quarter Quell; audience reviewers wrote of bawling their eyes out several times and of needing the film to slow down to give the characters more depth.

 SubjectiveNerdism — Sunrise on the Reaping reviews and Rotten Tomatoes score, updated November 21, 2026Nerdism's roundup, updated November 21, records the reviews going live November 17: about 69 to 72 percent on Rotten Tomatoes as the first 50 to 70 reviews were counted, and 56 of 100 on Metacritic, mixed or average. It files the Hollywood Reporter's David Rooney calling Joseph Zada's Haymitch far more involving than young Snow in the last prequel, the New York Times finding the film both bloated and limited, Variety's Owen Gleiberman calling it meandering and more than a bit thin while rating it fresh, the Guardian's Peter Bradshaw at one star, and Deadline questioning whether the franchise is running out of steam.

 SubjectiveCultural Watchlist — critics split on Sunrise on the ReapingThe Cultural Watchlist roundup of the November 17 reviews records a sharply divided verdict with one consensus: Joseph Zada's young Haymitch is a breakout success across otherwise irreconcilable reviews, Rooney's worthier prequel delivering on emotion and brutal spectacle at one pole and Bradshaw's dismissal at the other, IndieWire's Ryan Lattanzio between them on an overlong, visually soupy and narratively morose reprisal, and the New York Times' Brandon Yu framing the film as satisfying the formulaic thrills of young adult fantasy.

 SubjectiveIndy100 — what are critics saying about Sunrise on the Reaping?Indy100 records the prequel, based on Suzanne Collins's 2025 book and set 24 years before the original films on the morning of the reaping of the 50th Hunger Games, with Joseph Zada as Haymitch and Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Whitney Peak, Mckenna Grace, Maya Hawke and Kelvin Harrison Jr. in the cast. It files Rooney on Zada's tenacity, kindness and heartrending vulnerability, Yu's both bloated and limited, Gleiberman's meandering and thin in the lavish Hunger Games Classic mode, and Bradshaw's verdict that the film has no authentic reason to exist other than to gouge an income stream from its fanbase, and records an early critics' score of 75 percent and an IMDb mark of 7.4 of 10.

 SubjectiveDeadline via StupidDope — Sunrise on the Reaping box office opening weekend, November 21, 2026The box office account, carrying Deadline's Saturday morning update of November 21, records the film opening in about 4,018 North American locations, the largest opening screen count in Lionsgate history, making $56 million on Friday including $21.25 million in Thursday previews and projected at $120 million or more for the weekend, No. 1 in 66 of the 67 markets it had opened in. It records the audience side of the split in the same figures: 95 percent on Rotten Tomatoes, a franchise record ahead of Catching Fire at 89 percent, an A-minus CinemaScore, and PostTrak at 93 percent positive with 80 percent saying they would definitely recommend it, against a critics' mark of 68 percent.

 SubjectiveMovie Opinions — what to watch November 20: Sunrise on the Reaping and moreThe weekend guide, checked November 19, records exactly two wide openers on Cinema United's calendar: Sunrise on the Reaping across roughly 3,900 screens including every IMAX and premium format, at 158 minutes the longest film in the franchise, at 70 percent before sliding to 69 percent from 62 reviews; and I Play Rocky expanding to 2,000 theatres after a limited run averaging $17,024 per theatre, at 87 percent certified fresh with critics and 98 percent with audiences, opening one day before the 50th anniversary of Rocky's 1976 release, with tracking toward about $12 million.

### Bahrain Says a Civilian Plant Burned While the Guards Claim Two Patriot Radars in the Night, the Sparta II's Tow Still Stands Unconfirmed, and the Strait Opens Sunday With No Crossing Counted at the Stamp

Filed as: Edition No. 76 — The Overnight Watch · 2026-11-22T04:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-22-overnight-watch.html

The Night File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Bahrain Says a Civilian Plant Burned While the Guards Claim Two Patriot Radars in the Night, the Sparta II’s Tow Still Stands Unconfirmed, and the Strait Opens Sunday With No Crossing Counted at the Stamp

 The night file: one attack in the Gulf told two ways—two radars destroyed in Tehran’s account, a civilian plant afire in Manama’s, and no American word in the file at the stamp; a burning ship whose tow was promised for the night and is not confirmed in any account the desk read; a strait that opens Sunday at zero in one reading of its counter and one in another; a coin that would not hold its line through the night; a grounded bulker ballasted down against the weather with her last people lifted off; and a French law still waiting on the referral its opponents promise. Sunday carries the Review of Reviews.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0400 ET, Sunday, November 22, 2026. This edition continues the file from Edition No. 75, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 today, from Edition No. 74, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Saturday, from Edition No. 73, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 on Saturday, and from Edition No. 71, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 on Saturday. The Saturday Culture Feature, collected at 0410 on Saturday, stands in the Weekend Features. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the overnight figures differ from the earlier figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Night in Brief: One Attack in the Gulf in Two Tellings, a Tow That No Account Confirms, and a Strait at Zero

The night’s file is an attack on Bahrain that its two principals describe as two different attacks, a burning ship in the Baltic whose promised tow no account in the file confirms, and a strait that opens Sunday with no crossing counted in one reading of its counter and one crossing in another. Bahrain’s interior ministry reports an Iranian attack on a civilian industrial facility—fire, material damage, no injuries, the site unnamed—in the agency account filed below and in the Europe account filed below. The Revolutionary Guards, in a statement carried by IRNA, claim a combined missile and drone attack on United States positions at the Al-Riffa and Awali bases and the destruction of two Patriot radars, in the strikes account filed below. No United States confirmation of damage to any American equipment stands in the file at the stamp, in the dossier account filed below. The Sparta II’s tow, promised for Saturday night in the defence minister’s words, is not reported begun or done in any account the desk read; Finland’s prime minister said the war is spilling over, in the Baltic account filed below. The strait’s news brief records no crossing yet on Sunday as of 06:27 UTC, in the strait count filed below, while the same counter’s traffic table lists one, in the traffic account filed below—the desk prints the disagreement in the Cocked Hat. The desk takes the files in that order.

What the night settled is narrow: that Bahrain was attacked and a fire burned at a site Manama calls civilian; that alerts were issued, lifted and issued again; that interceptions were made, in Bahrain’s account; and that the week’s gold loss is a closed figure. What it left open is the rest: what was actually hit in Bahrain, whether the Sparta II moved in the night, the strait’s true Sunday count, the Darnytskyi’s damage, and every dated step of the week ahead, beginning with the North Atlantic Council on Monday.

The Gulf at 0400: Radars in Tehran’s Account, a Civilian Plant in Manama’s, and No American Word in the File

The Gulf’s overnight file opens where the week’s Bahrain file has stood since November 13—with the island attacked and the accounts apart—and adds missiles to a series that had run on drones. Bahrain’s interior ministry said an Iranian attack struck a civilian industrial facility on Saturday, starting a fire that Civil Defence teams worked to contain, with material damage and no injuries, and it did not name the facility or its location, in the agency account above and in the Munich account filed below. Residents saw smoke rising over Sitra Island, home to industrial sites including the state oil company’s refinery, in the agency account. The ministry’s night ran in alerts: a first alert urging residents to move to the nearest safe location, an all-clear, and then a second alert, in the interceptions account filed below. The Defence Force said its air defences intercepted a number of Iranian aerial attacks and that shrapnel from the interceptions caused material damage but no casualties, in the same accounts.

Tehran’s account names different targets and a different result. The Guards’ Aerospace Force carried out a combined missile-and-drone attack on United States positions at the Al-Riffa and Awali bases and struck the radars of two Patriot air defence systems, in the strikes account and in the claims account filed below. The Guards presented the strike as retaliation: for violations of Iranian airspace by United States MQ-1 and MQ-9 drones earlier that day, in the verification account filed below, and for an attack on a radar installation on Iran’s Hengam Island, in the dossier account. The Guards provided no evidence of damage to the radars, in the verification account, and neither the United States military nor Bahrain had confirmed damage to any American equipment by the early hours of Sunday, in the dossier account. Inside Iran’s own file the targets divide: the Fars agency named the Shaikh Isa and Al Juffair bases rather than Al-Riffa and Awali, in the strikes account, and IRNA carried a third version, that an interceptor missile launched from the Fifth Fleet base came down on Sitra Island and set off a large fire, in the fire account filed below. The available accounts do not establish whether the industrial site and the reported radar targets were separate locations, in the verification account. The desk prints the three tellings in the Cocked Hat and resolves none of them. The operation is the first in the series since November 13 in which Iran has claimed missiles as well as drones, in the dossier account.

The blockade’s file stands where the week left it, with its convoy unmoved in the night’s reading. More than 14 tankers stand gathered at Kharg Island to test the blockade, in the morning account filed below and in the Kharg account filed below; no Iranian official has confirmed a departure date, in the same account, and no departure stands in the overnight file. The one independent count in the file cuts the other way: nine large ships at anchor in the latest cloud-free frame of November 17, most parked since October, in the imagery digest filed below. A tracking firm’s second word on its own first report stands in the file: “Wishful thinking. That’s definitely not what’s going on,” in the convoy account filed below, which also records 31 laden sanctioned tankers already past the strait, holding in the Arabian Sea. Foreign Minister Araghchi’s condition stands as the midnight file printed it: as long as Iran’s demands are not met, discussion of the strait’s opening is pointless, in the morning account. Settled: the attack, the fire, the alerts and the claim. Open: the targets, the damage, and any American answer.

The Baltic at 0400: A Tow Promised for the Night and Not Confirmed at the Stamp, and a Prime Minister’s Word for the Spread

The Baltic file ends the night one announcement past the midnight stamp and no fact past it. The Sparta II, struck by two drones west of Gogland on Saturday morning, anchored off Loviisa and still burning at the turn of the log, was to be towed out of Finland’s territorial waters on Saturday night, in Defence Minister H&auml;kk&auml;nen’s statement to Helsingin Sanomat, as the midnight file printed it. No account in the overnight file reports the tow begun, completed or postponed, and the desk files the ship exactly where the evening left her: at anchor, burning, her 16 crew in Russia. What the night added is the frame around her. Prime Minister Orpo said on X that “the war is spilling over into our neighbouring areas,” that Finnish authorities are handling the situation in the Gulf of Finland, and that Ukraine has the right to fight against the aggressor, in the Baltic account. President Stubb called the events serious and said he was in close contact with the country’s foreign and security leadership, in the wire account the search file carried. Swedish combat aircraft, operating under Finnish command, took part in safeguarding Finland’s and the alliance’s territorial integrity, in Sweden’s defence minister’s word, in the Baltic account and in the spillover account filed below. Finland twice imposed temporary air and sea traffic restrictions as a precaution against stray drones, and the Estonian vessel Kindral Kurvits deployed at Finland’s request, in the summary account filed below, which also names the crew’s ship: the Kapitan Sakharov, which took the 16 from their liferaft.

On the crew, the night’s accounts divide, and the division is filed as it stands. The Border Guard’s account, carried in every Western file, has the crew evacuated in lifeboats to a Russian vessel and on their way home. Kaliningrad’s governor, Mr. Besprozvannykh, wrote that a Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, that the crew was carrying out the necessary work and planned to continue on its way, in the governor account filed below; the same account records the governor’s preliminary finding of two drones and no threat to the territory’s supplies. On the ship herself, one account adds the sanctions history whole: the European Union sanctioned her owner and never the ship, which kept the St. Petersburg–Kaliningrad run past four allied coasts, in the sanctions account filed below; coastguard commanders said the vessel was known to have carried weapons and that nobody yet knows what is in her containers this time, in the same account. The strike’s position is given three ways in the file—international waters west of Gogland in Finland’s placing, about 11 nautical miles north of Vaindloo in Estonia’s, and three nautical miles from the Russian border in the Leningrad governor’s—in the summary account. The suspected helicopter violation stands under investigation at 4.1 kilometres near Loviisa at about 12:34, in the same account. Kyiv has claimed nothing in any account in the file. Settled: the strike, the drift, the anchorage, the evacuation in the Finnish account, and the allied patrols. Open: the tow, the cargo, the crew’s two tellings, and responsibility in Kyiv’s word.

The Strait at 0400: No Crossing in the Brief, One in the Table, and a Week Revised Downward Twice

Sunday opens in the strait at the level the crisis has made normal, and its instruments open in disagreement with themselves. The counter’s news brief, updated at 06:27 UTC, records no identification-system-visible commercial ship crossed on Sunday yet, with Saturday closed at 12 crossings—eight inbound, four outbound, one a tanker, the last the Ocean Lion inbound at 21:22 UTC—and the seven-day figure at 54, an average of 7.7 a day, about 9 percent of the pre-crisis 84.8, the status severely restricted, in the strait count above. The same counter’s traffic table lists one crossing today: the bulk carrier Lolo Gate, outbound at 06:13 UTC bound for Kandla, with the seven-day figure at 55 and eight crossings in the last 24 hours, in the traffic account above. The midnight file closed the week at 56. Three readings of one instrument in nine hours—56, 55 and 54—stand in the Cocked Hat, unmerged. The second instrument counts a wider sea: 22 ships crossed in the 24 hours to 06:01 UTC, 13 in and nine out, with tankers carrying an estimated 1.09 million barrels out, in the monitor account filed below. The counter counts ships visible on the identification system and states plainly that ships sailing dark are missed.

The struck ships end the night where the midnight file left them. The Torkel burns at anchor under NAVAREA IX Warning 457/26 at 26 degrees 23.40 minutes north, 056 degrees 18.60 minutes east, in the situation report filed below; the Arina, hit in her engine room 50 minutes after the Torkel was hit on her stern, stands named in specialist reporting only, in the same report; and Friday’s ship, struck on her port bow eight nautical miles north of Khasab, ends her second night unnamed in every account in the file. Three ships in about 15 hours, in the situation report’s count; two named, one not; no casualties in any of the three. Settled: Saturday’s count at 12 in both readings of the counter, and the Torkel’s position. Open: Sunday’s first crossing, the Arina’s state, Friday’s name, and the true count of the strait.

The Markets at 0400: A Coin on Both Sides of Its Line, a Whale Buying the Low, and Gold’s Closed Week

Sunday’s only market is the one that never closes, and it spent the night on both sides of the line it retook on Saturday. The readings stand as the file gives them: $60,020.43 at 11:00 a.m. Korea time, up 1.85 percent over 24 hours, in the prices account filed below, in CoinMarketCap data; a last completed four-hour close of $60,365.70 and a captured quote of $60,214.70 at 00:19 UTC, against a $61,000 ceiling the rebound has not taken, in the chart account filed below; near $59,200 early on Sunday in CoinGecko’s quote, in the gold account filed below; $59,330 at 12:17 UTC+8, up 6.22 percent over 24 hours and down 8.48 percent over seven days, in the whales account filed below; and $59,124.06 at 07:58 UTC on the exchange’s day, which opened at $57,998.52 and ran from $57,381.45 to $60,996, in the exchange account filed below. One buyer stands named in the night’s file: Abraxas Capital Management withdrew 17,597 bitcoin, about $1.04 billion at an average price of about $59,206, from centralised exchanges while the coin traded below $60,000, in the on-chain tracker’s count in the whales account, of which 11,241 bitcoin were withdrawn as the price rebounded, in the analyst EmberCN’s count in the same account. The week’s liquidation figure stands at $1.8 billion in the gold account’s data, as the midnight file printed it. The futures reopen today at 1800 Eastern; nothing in a Sunday night quote settles Monday’s open.

Gold’s week, by contrast, is a closed book, and the overnight file carries its final figures. Front-month Comex gold lost 9.47 percent on the week to $3,512.30, the largest one-week decline since the week ending March 20, 2026, down 13.59 percent over two weeks and at its lowest settlement since August 29, 2025, in the data account filed below. The spot readings run lower in figure and near in kind: about 8.7 percent lost in five sessions, the week closing near $3,544, about 37 percent below the January 29 intraday peak near $5,600, in the slump account filed below, which carries a newsletter’s estimate of about $15 trillion in combined gold and silver value lost. The metal fell alongside equities and the coin, not against them, in both accounts—the week’s pattern, printed as the file states it. Settled: the week’s loss, in every instrument. Open: Monday’s open, on a week that begins with a council in Brussels and a short market week in Washington.

France at 0400: A Bulker Ballasted Down With Her Generators Dead, and a Law Still Waiting on Its Referral

The Landes file gained its machinery overnight and no movement. The Miro G, aground on sand near Lit-et-Mixe since 00:55 on Friday, has had her ballast tanks filled with seawater to improve her stability and reduce the risk of capsizing or moving farther toward the beach; the water must eventually be pumped out to lighten her before she can be pulled free, in the salvage account filed below. Her two main generators have failed, disrupting power to the pumps, and engineers are working to restore an alternative supply, in the same account. The salvage tug Abeille Bretagne has arrived with a 1,000-metre towline and cannot approach closer than about 900 metres in the shallow water, in the same account. The ship’s company thinned further on Saturday: after the 19 crew airlifted off on Friday, another 11 people—the captain, two other crew members, salvage experts and company representatives among them—were lifted off by helicopter ahead of deteriorating weather, in the digest account filed below, where the overnight file’s earlier standing of three remaining aboard no longer holds. Strong winds and rough seas are expected to continue, officials said refloating could take several days or longer, and no account promises success at the first weather window, in the salvage account. No pollution has been detected; she carries a little over a hundred tonnes of diesel, in the grounding account filed below. Settled: the ballast, the generators, the tug’s distance, and the empty ship. Open: the refloating.

Paris’s file did not move, and the desk records the standing with one consequence the night’s reading adds. The police firearms law, adopted Friday by 205 votes to 110, creates the rebuttable presumption and amends Article L.435-1; it has not been promulgated and has not entered into force, in the text account filed below. The consequence the overnight account states plainly: officers and gendarmes who have fired a lethal shot will no longer automatically be placed in custody, in the custody account filed below. The Senate left announced it would refer the matter to the Constitutional Council to block promulgation, in the same account; no filing of the referral stands in the overnight file, as at the midnight stamp. Promulgation should follow within 15 days unless the Council is seized, in the text account. Settled: the vote, the text and the custody consequence. Open: the referral, and the Council’s word.

Kyiv and Madrid at 0400: A Quiet Night in the File, a Toll That Stands, and a Campaign Eight Days Out

Ukraine’s overnight file is a quiet one, and the desk records the quiet as a quiet. No account in the file reports a new overnight strike on Ukraine between the midnight stamp and this one. Thursday night’s toll stands unrevised at at least nine killed—seven in Kyiv and two in Lviv—with the package at over 110 missiles and more than 400 drones, defences suppressing three ballistic missiles, 79 cruise missiles and 380 drones, and strikes recorded at 23 locations, in the bridges account filed below, whose information is verified through November 21. The bridges end the night in the two states the file has carried since Friday: all three closed to traffic in the BBC’s account, and traffic from the western to the eastern bank restored over the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi by mid-afternoon in Kyiv’s, with the Darnytskyi assessment still under way and no account giving its structural damage or a repair timetable for any crossing. Kryvyi Rih’s toll stands at two dead and 60 wounded, as the midnight file closed it. The North Atlantic Council meets in Brussels on Monday, with Warsaw’s guarantee given in person on Saturday. Settled: the standing. Open: the Darnytskyi, and what the Council does.

Spain’s file closes its Saturday with the count agreed and the warning given. The bullring filled: 12,000 attendees on the party’s count, in the rally account filed below, and around 12,000 with the arena full in the public broadcaster’s reporting, in the broadcaster account filed below—the party’s ninth filling of the ring, on about 300 buses, in the rally account. Mr. Feij&oacute;o’s word at the rally was a caution against his own side’s weather: do not trust the polls or the internal atmosphere, he said, for the other side is “capable of anything” and “wounded people are even more dangerous,” in the same account. The campaign average of 19 institutes stands at 30.9 for the People’s Party, 27.9 for the Socialists, 19.0 for Vox, 6.3 for Frente Amplio and 2.6 for ERC, in the same account. Sunday takes Mr. Feij&oacute;o to Murcia and Monday to C&aacute;diz, in the campaign file the desk has carried. Spain votes on November 29; Vox has reserved the same bullring for its closing rally on November 27, in the rally account. Settled: the count and the average. Open: whether either moves before Sunday week.

Sunday Ahead: The Review of Reviews, a Council on Monday, and the Futures at 1800

Sunday carries the paper’s Review of Reviews, the week’s books read through their reviewers, filed in the Weekend Features. It also carries the Sparta II’s tow, whenever it moves; the strait’s first full Sunday count; and the futures’ reopening at 1800 Eastern, the first market word on the week. The week ahead carries the North Atlantic Council in Brussels on Monday; the Senate Commerce Committee’s technical answers on the November 13 ground stop, due November 23; Virginia’s measles dashboard on November 24; Alaska’s certification on November 25; the October PCE reading, the second estimate of third-quarter product and the Beige Book on Wednesday, in a market week closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and closing early Friday; Spain’s second debate, about November 26, and its general election on November 29, the day the OPEC+ ministers also meet; the House committees’ closed-door interview with Nvidia’s former chief executive on December 1; the Federal Reserve’s decision on December 8 and 9; and the end of government funding after December 11. The Midday Watch collects at 1200.

The Cocked Hat

Where the night’s bearings do not meet, the desk prints the triangle. On Bahrain’s night: two Patriot radars struck at Al-Riffa and Awali, in the Guards’ statement; a civilian industrial facility afire with no injuries and the site unnamed, in the Interior Ministry’s account; a fire on Sitra Island caused by an interceptor missile from the Fifth Fleet base, in IRNA’s version; and the targets named as Shaikh Isa and Al Juffair, in the Fars agency’s. On the interceptions: a number of aerial attacks intercepted with shrapnel damage, in the Defence Force’s account; and no United States confirmation of damage to any American equipment in any account at the stamp. On the Sparta II’s crew: evacuated by liferaft to a Russian vessel and bound home, in the Border Guard’s account; and told a rescue vessel they did not need evacuation and planned to continue on their way, in the Kaliningrad governor’s. On her strike position: west of Gogland, in Finland’s placing; 11 nautical miles north of Vaindloo, in Estonia’s; three nautical miles from the Russian border, in the Leningrad governor’s. On the strait’s Sunday: no crossing yet as of 06:27 UTC, in the counter’s news brief; one crossing, the Lolo Gate outbound at 06:13 UTC, in the same counter’s traffic table; and 22 ships in the 24 hours to 06:01 UTC, in the monitor. On its week: 54 crossings in the brief, 55 in the table, and 56 as the midnight file closed it. On the Kharg convoy: more than 14 tankers gathered and crewed, in the imagery reporting; nine large ships at anchor, most parked since October, in the digest’s own count of the November 17 frame. On Bitcoin at the stamp: $60,020.43 at 0200 Eastern in one data service, $59,124.06 at 0258 Eastern in the exchange’s day, and near $59,200 early Sunday in a third quote. On gold’s week: down 9.47 percent in the front-month contract, down about 8.7 percent in the spot readings. Inside the triangle is where the night honestly stands, and the log turns on it.

 The Clippings Filed With This Edition

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 38 items.

 
 SubjectiveStatement, carrying the agency file — Bahrain says Iran struck industrial siteBahrain accused Iran on Saturday of striking a civilian industrial facility, causing a fire and damage to property, with no injuries reported. The interior ministry said Civil Defence was working to bring the fire under control and did not disclose where the facility was. Residents told the agency they had seen smoke rising over Sitra Island, on the country’s east coast, which is home to several industrial sites, including a refinery run by the state-owned oil company Bapco. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards announced that they had carried out missile and drone strikes on United States military positions at the Al-Riffa and Awali bases in Bahrain.

 SubjectiveDevdiscourse — Bahrain says Iranian attack hits industrial facility as air defences intercept attacksBahrain said on Saturday that an Iranian attack had hit a civilian industrial facility, causing a fire but no injuries, while Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they launched a missile-and-drone attack on United States military positions in the kingdom, home to the United States Navy’s Fifth Fleet. The interior ministry first issued an alert urging residents to move to the nearest safe location, later issued an all-clear, and then sent a second alert. The Defence Force said its air defences had intercepted a number of Iranian aerial attacks, and that shrapnel from the interceptions caused material damage but no casualties. The Guards, in a statement carried by the state news agency IRNA, said their aerospace forces had launched a combined missile-and-drone attack on United States positions at the Al-Riffa and Awali bases.

 SubjectiveGlobeNow — Iran strikes US bases in Bahrain with missiles and drones, Bahrain says factory hitIran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Saturday night they had launched missile and drone strikes on American military positions in Bahrain. The Guards said the attack had hit the radars of two American Patriot air defence systems, and described it as retaliation for continued aggression and repeated violations of Iranian airspace. Bahrain’s interior ministry said a civilian industrial facility had been targeted and a fire had broken out; Civil Defence teams worked to bring the blaze under control, and the ministry said there were no injuries, only material damage. The Defence Force said its air defences had intercepted a number of Iranian aerial attacks and that falling debris caused damage on the ground but no casualties. The Guards’ statement named the Al-Riffa and Awali Sakhir bases, while the Fars news agency reported earlier that the Shaikh Isa and Al Juffair bases had been attacked.

 SubjectivePollar News — Iranian attack sparks fire at Bahrain industrial siteBahrain’s Interior Ministry said on Saturday, November 21, that an Iranian attack had struck a civilian industrial facility and started a fire, describing the strike as Iranian aggression and reporting material damage with no injuries; the ministry did not name the facility or say where it was located. The Revolutionary Guards said they had carried out a combined missile and drone operation against United States military positions at the al-Riffa and Awali bases and destroyed two United States Patriot air defence radars there. The Fars news agency named a different pair of targets, the Sheikh Isa and Juffair bases. IRNA gave a different version, saying an interceptor missile launched from the United States Fifth Fleet base in Bahrain had come down on Sitra Island and set off a large fire. The Defence Force said its air defences had intercepted several Iranian aerial attacks on the night of November 21.

 SubjectiveSilent Dossier — Iran Strikes Bahrain: Guards Claim Two Patriot Radars HitThe Revolutionary Guards claimed a combined missile and drone attack on American forces at the Al-Riffa and Awali bases late on November 21, stating that its Aerospace Force struck the radars of two United States Army Patriot air defence systems. The Guards presented the strike as retaliation for violations of Iranian airspace by United States MQ-1 and MQ-9 drones earlier that day, and for an attack on a radar installation on Iran’s Hengam Island. Neither the United States military nor Bahrain had confirmed damage to any American equipment by the early hours of November 22, with Bahrain reporting instead that the attack set fire to a civilian industrial facility. The operation follows at least two Guards drone attacks on the island since November 13, and is the first in that series in which Iran has claimed missiles as well as drones. Accounts circulated in Iran named Isa Air Base and the Juffair naval district rather than Al-Riffa and Awali as the targets.

In a statement carried by its official outlet Sepah News on Saturday night, the Guards said its aerospace force struck two United States Patriot air defence radars at the Al-Riffa and Awali Sakhir air bases. Bahrain’s Defence Force said its air defence systems had intercepted several Iranian aerial attacks; falling debris caused minor material damage but no casualties.  SubjectiveBulletin Observer — Bahrain reports fire as Iran claims US Patriot radar strikesThe Revolutionary Guard said it struck two United States Patriot radars in Bahrain with missiles and drones on Saturday night, November 21. Bahrain reported a fire at a civilian industrial facility, but damage to the radars has not been independently verified. The Guards named the Al-Riffa and Awali Sakhir bases as the targets and said the strikes were retaliation for United States MQ-1 and MQ-9 drones entering Iranian airspace earlier that day, an allegation that has not been independently verified. The Guards did not provide evidence of damage to the radars. The Interior Ministry said a fire broke out at the industrial facility, and the available accounts do not establish whether that site and the reported radar targets were separate locations. Reports also differed over which bases were attacked: the Guards named Al-Riffa and Awali Sakhir, while the Fars news agency separately named Shaikh Isa and Al Juffair.

 SubjectiveBrussels Reporter — Salvage teams assess grounded cargo ship off FranceA Maltese-flagged cargo ship remains stranded off southwestern France as authorities work to prevent it from capsizing and causing pollution, with salvage experts assessing how to refloat it. The 169-metre Miro G ran aground near Cap de l’Homy in the Landes department, close to Lit-et-Mixe, shortly before 1 a.m. on Friday, November 20. The ship’s ballast tanks have been filled with seawater to improve stability and reduce the risk of capsizing or moving farther toward the beach; the water will eventually have to be pumped out to lighten the vessel so it can be pulled free. The ship’s two main generators have failed, disrupting power to the pumps, and engineers are working to restore an alternative electricity supply. The salvage tug Abeille Bretagne has arrived with a 1,000-metre towline; shallow water prevents it from coming closer than about 900 metres to the stranded ship. Strong winds and rough seas are expected to continue, and officials said refloating could take several days or longer, with no guarantee the operation would succeed.

 SubjectivegCaptain — Crew Airlifted After Bulk Carrier Grounds on French CoastThe 169-metre Miro G grounded near Lit-et-Mixe in southwestern France’s Landes region shortly after midnight on November 20, after its crew reported difficulty manoeuvring in deteriorating weather. Nineteen of the vessel’s 22 crew members were evacuated by a French Air and Space Force helicopter operating from Cazaux. A French Navy evaluation and intervention team was deployed by helicopter to assess the ship’s condition, a Falcon 50 surveillance aircraft monitored the vessel and found no evidence of pollution, and the emergency towing vessel Abeille Bretagne departed Brest in anticipation of a refloating operation. The vessel carries more than 100 tonnes of diesel fuel. Options under consideration include pumping fuel from the vessel to reduce its weight before attempting to tow it into deeper water. The ship, built in 2011 with a deadweight of about 28,200 tonnes, was sailing without cargo and was reportedly bound for Rouen to load about 30,000 tonnes of wheat for Libya. The incident triggered Level 3 of France’s maritime emergency response and the Franco-Spanish Biscaye Plan.

 SubjectiveThe Fact Wire — Text changes how police and gendarmerie shootings are examinedAdopted on Friday by Parliament, the text establishes a presumption of lawful use of weapons for police officers and gendarmes. As a consequence of the presumption, gendarmes and police officers who have fired a lethal shot will no longer automatically be placed in custody. The text changes the framework in which shots fired by police officers and gendarmes are examined, while the number of gunshots and the conduct of investigations after a lethal use of a weapon remain at the heart of the debate. Opponents consider the measure dangerous for fundamental rights. The Senate left, hostile to the text, announced that it would refer the matter to the Constitutional Council to block its promulgation.

 SubjectiveBars Across — France Approves Rebuttable Presumption for Police Firearms UseFrance has approved a bill creating a rebuttable presumption that national police officers and gendarmes used firearms lawfully. The Senate adopted it on November 20, 2026, by 205 votes to 110, with 27 abstentions and six senators not voting; the National Assembly approved the text in July 2026. It has not yet been promulgated or entered into force. It amends Article L.435-1 of the Internal Security Code; firearms use remains permitted in five situations, every use must remain absolutely necessary and strictly proportionate, the presumption covers national police and gendarmes and not municipal police, and any contrary evidence may rebut it. An opinion of November 5 from the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe’s democracy office recommended reconsidering the measure. The Socialist, Ecologist and Republican group says it will refer the bill to the Constitutional Council before promulgation; no court has ruled on its constitutionality, and promulgation should follow within 15 days unless the Council is seized.

### Saturday Closes With the Sparta II Still Burning and a Tow Promised in the Night, the Strait's Two Tankers Named—the Torkel Burning at Anchor and the Arina Hit in Her Engine Room—and Bitcoin Holding $60,000 at the Turn of the Log

Filed as: Edition No. 75 — The Midnight Watch · 2026-11-22T00:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-22-midnight-watch.html

The Midnight File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Saturday Closes With the Sparta II Still Burning and a Tow Promised in the Night, the Strait’s Two Tankers Named—the Torkel Burning at Anchor and the Arina Hit in Her Engine Room—and Bitcoin Holding $60,000 at the Turn of the Log

 The last entry of the day, filed before the log turns: a ship burning at anchor with a tow promised in the night and no word at the stamp that it had moved; two tankers named at last in one sea and Friday’s ship still unnamed; a hometown’s toll unrevised; a diplomacy whose two sentences still do not meet; a port strike averted on the Pacific coast; and a coin that found its floor at $55,130 and held $60,000 into the turn.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Sunday, November 22, 2026. This edition closes the day continued in Edition No. 74, the Evening Watch, collected at 1800 on Saturday, in Edition No. 73, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 on Saturday, in Edition No. 71, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 on Saturday, and in Edition No. 70, the Midnight Watch, collected at 0000 on Saturday. The Saturday Culture Feature, collected at 0410 on Saturday, stands in the Weekend Features. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight figures differ from the evening figures, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Midnight in Brief: What Saturday Settled, What It Left Open

Saturday settled the names of the strait’s two tankers, the day’s final crossing count, the terms each side demands in the open, and the level at which the coin closed—and left a burning ship’s tow, a hometown’s next count, and Monday’s council open at the turn of the log. The two tankers struck off Khasab in the morning are the Torkel and the Arina, two Hong Kong-flagged suezmaxes identified in specialist reporting, in the names account filed below, with the Torkel alone carried in an official navigational warning, burning at anchor, in the situation report filed below. The Sparta II ends the day where the evening left her—at anchor off Loviisa, still burning, her crew in Russia—with one addition: Finland’s defence minister said she would be towed out of Finnish waters in the night, in the eighteen-outlet account filed below, and no account in the file at the stamp says the tow began. Saturday’s visible crossings close at 12, in the strait count filed below. Bitcoin closes the day at $60,094, in the closing account filed below. The desk takes the files in that order.

What Saturday settled is the Torkel’s name, position and fire; the Arina’s name in specialist reporting; the visible count at 12 and the week at 56; Tehran’s conditions, listed in full for the first time in the file; Virginia’s standing and the Fifth Circuit’s, neither moved; a tentative agreement that averts a strike at the two Pacific ports; and the coin’s close. What it left open is the rest: whether the tow moved the Sparta II, Friday’s tanker’s name, the Darnytskyi’s damage, the strait’s true count, and every dated step of the week ahead.

The Baltic at Midnight: A Fire Still Burning, a Tow Promised, and No Word That It Moved

The Baltic file ends Saturday one fact past the evening. The Sparta II, struck by two drones west of Gogland between 0840 and 0850 local time, anchored south of Loviisa at 1545, her 16 crew evacuated to a Russian ship and on their way home, was still burning late on Saturday with Finland leading the rescue operation, in the Baltic account filed below. The addition is the tow. Defence Minister Antti Hakkanen told Helsingin Sanomat that the Sparta II would be towed out of Finland’s territorial waters on Saturday night, in the eighteen-outlet account above and in the wire account filed below; the situation report carries the same plan in the Border Guard’s terms—transfer of the disabled vessel into Russia’s maritime area of responsibility by tow—with Finnish, Estonian and Russian response assets joined in the operation and a restricted area standing around the ship. No account in the file at the midnight stamp reports the tow under way, completed, or postponed. The day therefore closes with the ship’s removal announced and unconfirmed, and the desk files it exactly so.

On responsibility, the day’s last word is firmer than its first and still short of a claim. A Border Guard officer confirmed that a Ukrainian drone strike hit the ship in the morning and caused the fire, in the eighteen-outlet account; Finland’s armed forces spokesman’s judgement stands beside it—it is likely that Ukraine is behind the attack, with no conclusive evidence—in the Baltic account; and Kyiv has claimed nothing in any account in the file. The cargo stands undisclosed: there is no confirmed information about what is on board, and military materiel cannot be ruled out, the Border Guard’s commander said, in the same account; the vessel’s own record stands in the ship’s entry filed below—a roll-on/roll-off vessel shuttling between St. Petersburg and Kaliningrad since October 2022. The suspected helicopter violation stands as the evening filed it: about 4.1 kilometres inside Finnish territory near Loviisa shortly after midday, under Border Guard investigation. Settled: the strike, the drift, the anchorage, the evacuation, the fire at the turn, and the tow’s announcement. Open: the tow itself, the cargo, and responsibility in Kyiv’s word.

Ukraine at Midnight: A Toll Unrevised, Two Bridge States Standing, and a Council on Monday

Ukraine’s file did not move after the evening, and the desk records the standing as the day’s close. Kryvyi Rih’s toll stands unrevised at two dead—a boy of seven and a woman of 20—and 60 wounded, six of them children, with four fires and about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and an industrial facility damaged, in the wire account filed below. The sequence stands in the city administration’s words: two ballistic missiles first, then three more rockets on the doctors, rescuers and utility workers who answered. The night’s second field stands beside it: 11 people, including two children, wounded when a drone hit a five-storey apartment building in the Kharkiv region, in the toll account filed below, and the air force’s figures—three ballistic missiles and 148 drones launched in the night, 117 destroyed or jammed—stand unrevised. Thursday night’s national toll stands at at least nine killed, seven in Kyiv and two in Lviv, in the BBC account filed below.

The bridges end the day in the two states the file has carried since midday, and the midnight file does not merge them. All three struck crossings closed to traffic, in the BBC account; traffic from the western to the eastern bank restored over the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi bridge by mid-afternoon, with the Darnytskyi assessment still under way, in the accounts the midday file carried. No account in the day’s file gives the Darnytskyi’s structural damage or a repair timetable for any crossing. The argument over the other bridge ends the day in both capitals’ numbers, spoken in Kyiv: 109 Russian attacks on Ukrainian bridges, in President Zelensky’s count, in the briefing account filed below; several months to a year to clear the Crimean Bridge’s collapsed section, in his defence minister’s estimate, against one to two months for some road sections, in the Russian deputy prime minister’s estimate of November 19, in the 109 account filed below. Warsaw’s file stands as the evening left it: every inch guaranteed in person, adjustments promised, and the North Atlantic Council in Brussels on Monday, in the Warsaw account filed below. Settled: the toll and the argument. Open: the Darnytskyi, and what the Council does.

The Strait at Midnight: Two Ships Named, a Third Still Nameless, and the Day Counted at Twelve

The strait’s midnight gain is names. The tanker struck on her stern at 0500 UTC, 11 nautical miles north of Khasab, is the Torkel, a Hong Kong-flagged suezmax of 153,300 tons deadweight built in 2009, whose crew was evacuated after the attack, in the names account above; the tanker struck in her engine room 50 minutes later, 17 nautical miles east of Khasab, is the Arina, a Hong Kong-flagged suezmax of 159,400 tons built in 2003, with a fire started in her engine room, in the same account. The official record carries one of the two: NAVAREA IX Warning 457/26 reports the Torkel involved in a security incident, burning and anchored at 26 degrees 23.40 minutes north, 056 degrees 18.60 minutes east, with mariners cautioned around the position, in the situation report. The warnings beneath the names stand as the wire filed them—two incidents, no casualties in either, and not immediately clear whether they involved the same vessel, in the wire account filed below—and Tehran’s reading stands beside them: a tanker afire after hitting a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait, in the two-incidents account filed below. Friday’s ship, struck on her port bow eight nautical miles north of Khasab, ends the week as she began it: unnamed in every account in the file. Three ships in about 15 hours, in the situation report’s count; two named, one not.

The day’s traffic closes in the visible counter at 12 crossings—eight inbound, four outbound, one of them a tanker, the last the general cargo ship Ocean Lion, inbound at 2122 UTC—with Friday confirmed at 13 and the seven-day figure at 56, an average of 8.0 a day, about 9 percent of the pre-crisis 84.8, in the strait count. The 24-hour replay’s figure stands against it as the evening printed it: 24 ships in the 24 hours to 2131 UTC, in the replay account filed below. The two instruments do not count the same sea, and the desk does not merge them. The assessment file adds a second sea’s warning: the Houthis are reinforcing positions along the Bab al Mandeb with tunnels and berms, on the word of military and local sources, in the assessment account filed below, and a Houthi spokesman warned shipping companies to remove vessels from Saudi Red Sea ports if the coalition attacked Hodeidah, naming Jeddah, Yanbu, Jazan and the King Fahd Industrial Port, with no confirmed strike, closure or evacuation order at the report’s cutoff, in the situation report. Settled: Saturday’s two names in specialist reporting, the Torkel’s in the official warning, and the visible count at 12. Open: the Arina’s state, Friday’s name, and the true count.

The diplomacy ends the day with its terms, for the first time, listed whole on one side. Iran’s conditions include ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the United States counter-blockade of Iranian ports, in the talks account filed below; reopening the strait on those conditions is “not difficult,” Foreign Minister Araghchi said, and as long as Iran’s demands are not met, discussion of the opening is pointless, in the same account. The uranium stays: the enriched material will not leave the country, and the Islamabad memorandum is no longer on the table in its earlier form, while the two-day plan for the strait still stands, in the talks record filed below. Qatari mediators have travelled to Tehran, in the talks account. On the other side, the President told Fox News on Saturday that he wants a permanent deal that stops Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, called Iranian officials “very, very difficult,” and said, “We make a deal, and then they break the deal the next day,” in the talks account. Settled: both sides’ terms, in their own words, on the same day. Open: whether the listed conditions and the word permanent can ever describe the same agreement.

The appeal is certain and unfiled in the file, in the docket account filed below.

The day’s one American settlement arrived on the Pacific coast. The Pacific Maritime Association and ILWU Local 26 reached a tentative contract agreement on Saturday, averting the threatened watchmen’s strike at Los Angeles and Long Beach, in the situation report; the agreement covers about 250 port watchmen responsible for terminal access control, security patrols and safety reporting, the existing contract remains in force while the members consider ratification, the final terms were not published, and no work stoppage was reported. Settled, subject to a vote: the largest container-port complex in the country keeps its gates. The chipmaker’s file closes the day unmoved, as the evening left it: California’s investigative subpoena of November 19, the Commission’s reported accounting inquiry, the criminal investigation of Megaspeed beside the company, no charges on any front, no answer from the company, and a board that will not reinstate its former chief executive, in the subpoena account filed below. The Cocked Hat

Where the day’s bearings do not meet, the desk prints the triangle. On the Sparta II’s attacker: a Ukrainian drone strike confirmed, in a Border Guard officer’s word; Ukraine likely behind it with no conclusive evidence, in the armed forces spokesman’s judgement; and no claim from Kyiv in any account. On her removal: towed out of Finnish waters on Saturday night, in the defence minister’s statement to a newspaper; transfer by tow planned, in the situation report; and no account at the stamp of the tow begun or done. On the strait’s Saturday: 12 crossings in the visible counter’s completed day; 24 ships in the 24-hour replay to 2131 UTC. Inside the triangle is where Saturday honestly stands, and the log turns on it.

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. 35 items.

At that level the coin was about 12 percent below where it stood at the same hour on Friday, November 13, when it was priced at $68,314. The slide followed a week in which bitcoin traded above $70,000 early on and then broke below $65,000 on Tuesday, $62,000 on Thursday and $60,000 on Friday.
